title: Grades measure the test.
dek: Know 60 of 100 topics, get asked 10 at random: 15.38% of the time you score 8 or more, 15.38% of the time 4 or less. Same knowledge, different grade.
whyThisIdea: Este următoarea idee nefolosită din backlog (#22; am sărit din nou peste #1, #7 și #14, încă marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate). E mijlocul semestrului, când vin primele note, și continuă „Studying is not learning”: aritmetica (60 din 100 de subiecte știute, 10 trase la întâmplare) arată cât din notă e noroc, plus legea lui Goodhart pentru învățatul „pe subiecte”.

entry.title: Grades measure the test.
entry.dek: Know 60 of 100 topics, get asked 10 at random: 15.38% of the time you score 8 or more, 15.38% of the time 4 or less. Same knowledge, different grade.
body: “A grade tells you how you did on the test. It does not tell you what you know.”

Have you ever asked yourself what a grade actually measures? Today is Tuesday, the 17th of November, we are in the middle of the semester, and for anyone in school this is the time when the first tests come back. You look at the number, you feel good or bad for one evening, and you move on. I have done that my whole life. So the question is: when I get a 7, is that a measurement of what I know, or a measurement of one hour on one day? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is the grade itself, and I met it the same way everybody does - from the inside, as a student. Two weeks ago I wrote that studying is not learning, that the hours at the desk are not the same as what stays in your head. This is the other end of the same road. Even if something did stay in my head, the grade is the only part of it that anybody else will ever see. And I noticed that I trust that number much more than I should.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do. “The test” and “the knowledge”. The knowledge is everything I can do with a subject - every topic, every type of problem, every connection between them. The test is a small piece of that, chosen by somebody else, on a day chosen by somebody else, in one or two hours. A grade is not a picture of the whole subject, it is a picture of the small piece that happened to be asked. <u>The grade is a sample, and nobody tells you how big the sample was.</u>

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic, because this is where it surprised me. These numbers are an example I built, not a measurement. Let’s say a subject has 100 topics, and the exam picks 10 of them at random, one point for each. And let’s say I know exactly 60 of the 100 topics, no more, no less. What grade do I get? The honest answer is: it depends on which 10 come up. If I calculate it properly (with combinations, the same maths as a lottery):
chance of getting 8 or more: 15.38%
chance of getting 4 or less: 15.38%
Same person, same knowledge, same 60 topics. About 3 exams out of 20 I walk out with an 8, 9 or 10, and about 3 out of 20 with a 4 or less. The difference between “very good” and “failed” can be only the questions on the paper.

And it does not go away for the good students either. Let’s say my colleague knows 80 topics out of 100. The chance that the exam gives them 6 or less is 10.96%, so about one exam in nine. And a student who knows only 50 topics still has a 4.58% chance of getting 8 or more. Put those two people in the same room on the wrong day and the one who knows less can walk out with the better grade (yes, you read that right, with 30 topics less). Over many exams it evens out - over one, it does not, and most of the grades that matter are decided by one.

Now let’s change one thing. Let’s say the exam does not pick at random, and everybody knows that it usually asks the same 20 favourite topics from the past papers. A smart student learns only those 20 and gets a 10. Another student learns all 100 topics, not perfectly, and gets an 8. On paper the first one is better. In reality the first one knows 20% of the subject. This has a name. The economist Charles Goodhart wrote about it in 1975 about monetary policy, and the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later put it in the sentence everybody quotes: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” The moment I study for the grade instead of the subject, the grade stops telling me anything about the subject.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Grades are not useless, and I would be lying if I said they were. A teacher with thirty students cannot sit with each one for three hours and find out what they really know. A test is cheap, it is the same for everybody, and over a whole year, with many tests, the luck from one day mostly cancels out. In my example, the student who knows 80 topics beats the one who knows 50 almost every time - just not every single time. And without any number at all, I would probably think I know much more than I do, because that is exactly what I wrote about with re-reading - familiar feels like known. A grade is a bad portrait, but it is still better than a mirror that only shows you what you want to see.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. The next time a test comes back, before I look at the number, I will look at the questions I got wrong and ask one thing: “Did I not know this, or did I just not expect it?” The first one is about knowledge, and I can fix it. The second one is about the sample, and I can only make it smaller by knowing more of the subject, not more of the past papers. And when I get a good grade on something I know I learned badly, I will try to be honest and call it what it is: a good day.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that most of us read a grade as a verdict on what we know, when it is closer to a photo of one hour. But I have to be honest about two things. My arithmetic assumes that all topics are equal and that every question is just “know it or not”, and real exams are not that clean - a good teacher writes questions that test understanding, not luck. And it is easy for a student to say “grades do not measure anything” right after a bad one, so I do not fully trust myself on this either. What I take from it is smaller: use the grade to find the gaps, not to decide who you are.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“A grade tells you how you did on the test. It does not tell you what you know.”
